name: The Münchhausen Trilemma
statement: Every attempt to justify a claim ends in infinite regress, circularity, or an unjustified stopping point.
statementAccent: infinite regress, circularity, or an unjustified stopping point
meaning: The Münchhausen trilemma is the argument that no belief can be given a complete, non-question-begging justification. Any demand to justify a claim, and then to justify that justification, and so on, must end in one of three unsatisfactory ways: an infinite regress of reasons that is never completed, a circle in which the claim ultimately supports itself, or a dogmatic halt at some assumption asserted without further support. The name evokes Baron Münchhausen's tall tale of pulling himself out of a swamp by his own hair.
mechanism: Push any justification with the question 'and why believe that?' and the chain of reasons can only terminate in one of three ways. It can go on forever, an infinite regress that never delivers a foundation. It can loop back, so that a premise is eventually justified by the very conclusion it was meant to support, which is circular. Or it can stop at a claim taken as basic and simply not justified further, which is dogmatic. Since each horn fails the demand for complete rational justification, the trilemma concludes that such justification is impossible, and something other than proof must ground belief.

examples.text: Ask why the sky is blue, then why that explanation holds, and so on: the answers either never end, eventually assume what they set out to prove, or stop at an unjustified 'that is simply how it is.'
Attempts to ground all knowledge on self-evident first principles face the dogmatic horn — why accept the principles? — which is the trilemma applied to epistemology's foundations.
The ancient Sceptics catalogued this in the modes of Agrippa, which included regress, hypothesis, and circularity among five modes for suspending judgement.

variants.name: Foundationalism
variants.text: The response that accepts the third horn but denies it is vicious: some basic beliefs are properly basic and need no further justification, halting the regress legitimately rather than dogmatically.

variants.name: Coherentism
variants.text: The response that embraces a form of the second horn: justification is holistic, a belief is justified by its fit within a mutually supporting web, so large-scale circularity is a virtue, not a fault.

whyItMatters: It is a sharp statement of the regress problem, one of the oldest and most fundamental challenges in epistemology. By showing that every structure of justification faces the same three exits, it frames the central debate between foundationalism, coherentism, and infinitism, and it fuels philosophical scepticism about whether any belief can be conclusively rationally grounded. Any theory of knowledge must say which horn it takes and why that horn is not fatal.

working.text: keep asking why a justification holds, and watch which of the three exits the chain is heading toward.
recognise that any account of justification must accept a regress, a circle, or a stopping point, and be explicit about which.
if you halt at basic beliefs, give a reason they need no further support, rather than merely asserting them, to avoid the dogmatic charge.

limits: It is a contested argument, not a proof that knowledge is impossible: foundationalists deny that stopping at properly basic beliefs is dogmatic, coherentists deny that holistic circularity is vicious, and infinitists defend the regress, so each horn has serious defenders. Its provenance is layered — the ancient version is Agrippa's five modes, not three, and the modern three-horned framing and the Münchhausen name were given by Hans Albert in the twentieth century. Whether the trilemma genuinely defeats the possibility of justified belief, or merely maps the options for it, is itself debated.
misreadings: It does not prove that nothing can be known — it lays out three problematic structures of justification, each of which some serious theory of knowledge accepts and defends. It is not originally three-horned: the ancient Agrippan modes number five, and the trilemma is a modern distillation. And the name is Hans Albert's coinage, not an ancient title; Albert popularised the three-horned form, drawing on the older sceptical tradition.
origin: The modern three-horned formulation and the name were given by the German philosopher Hans Albert in 'Traktat über die kritische Vernunft' (1968), drawing on the ancient modes of Agrippa the Sceptic recorded by Sextus Empiricus.
